title: Misinformation and Profitability of Hepatitis B Virus Claims on Instagram: Formative Cross-Sectional Study
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of 103 top Instagram posts retrieved with the search terms 'hepatitis b' and 'hep b'; each post coded accurate vs misinformation by hepatology clinicians against current standards of care, giving a share of items classified as misinformation with a stated denominator (24/103, 23.3%).

estimates.country: worldwide (posts originated in the Americas 38.8%, Western Pacific 19.4%, Africa 15.2%, Southeast Asia 14.6%, European 6.8%, Eastern Mediterranean 4.9%)
estimates.measure_type: % of top Instagram posts about hepatitis B that contained misinformation
estimates.denominator: 103 unique publicly available Instagram posts: the top 55 posts returned for each of the search terms "hepatitis b" and "hep b", with duplicates removed
estimates.definition: Post evaluated by hepatology clinicians for the presence or absence of accurate information based on current standards of care, coded accurate (score=0) versus misinformation (score=1)
estimates.misinfo_def: "any health-related claim of fact that is false based on current scientific consensus"
estimates.source_quote: Of the full sample, most posts had accurate (79/103, 76.7%) versus inaccurate (24/103, 23.3%) information about HBV.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract (Results) and Results, "Prevalence of and Engagement With HBV Claims and Misinformation on Instagram", p. 5
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Adapted Online Cancer Nutrition Misinformation (OnC-M) codebook applied to 58 variables per post. Two coding cycles "to establish reliability": 10% of posts inductively coded by two authors (ZCW, AG), discrepancies resolved by consensus with a tiebreaker (ELW), then the codebook applied to the remainder; accuracy judged by hepatology clinicians against current standards of care. NO kappa or other inter-rater reliability coefficient is reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: In December 2021, we searched Instagram using key search terms "hepatitis b" and "hep b." ... To describe the most viewed content on Instagram, we collected the top 55 posts populated for each term. This procedure is standard, given that algorithmically the most popular and engaging posts (ie, most viewed and liked) are more likely to populate first [38]. ... We aimed for a sample of 100 posts, with oversampling each term to account for duplication; duplicates were removed, resulting in a final sample of 103 posts.
estimates.notes: Headline prevalence. Sample is rank-truncated (top 55 posts per search term), hence denom_selection=curated; the authors themselves warn it "cannot be generalized to the prevalence of HBV on Instagram over time". Country coded Global: posts came from six WHO regions, and searches were English-language, run by US-based researchers. year set to 2021 (searches began December 2021; extraction ran to January 2022). Topic is health_other (hepatitis B), not vaccines, despite 'vaccine' appearing as a keyword. Source quote replaced (it was an ellipsis join) with the contiguous abstract sentence. The Results restatement, "Nearly a quarter of posts (24/103, 23.3%) contained misinformation about hepatitis B and hepatitis B treatment.", is split across the two columns of the text rendering and cannot be quoted contiguously.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) A September 2025 replication is reported in the Limitations: "we conducted a small replication study in September 2025 (n=60 posts, 30 from each search term), which exhibited similar topics of misinformation and a nearly identical proportion of misinformation (33% of posts, compared to 30% in the original sample from December 2021)". I did NOT create a second row for it: the instruction is to collapse repeated time points to one representative point, n is small, no methods are given for the replication, and - importantly - the same sentence states the original proportion as 30%, which CONTRADICTS the 23.3% (24/103) reported everywhere else in the paper. That 30% appears to be a confusion with "With 30% of Instagram posts that had misinformation containing conspiracy theories". An adjudicator wanting the 2025 wave should treat 33% (n=60) as low confidence given this inconsistency. (2) Misinformation rates within claim-type subsets were NOT entered as rows (same measure, sub-corpora of the same 103 posts; entering them would inflate): activism 11/50 (22%), prevention 2/27 (7.4%), treatment 10/18 (55.6%), cure 9/12 (75%), natural remedies 12/13 (92.3%), symptoms 9/15 (60%), anecdote 5/10 (50%), censorship conspiracies 6/9 (66.7%), other 13/33 (39.4%). Each is an exact part/whole share of verbatim counts, so any of them could be recovered if the review wants topic-conditional rows. (3) "most posts had accurate (79/103, 76.7%)" is the exact complement of the kept row. (4) Within-misinformation shares that are not falsity measures: 39.5% (15/24) of misinformation posts were for-profit; 30% of misinformation posts contained conspiracy theories; 88.9% (8/9) of censorship-conspiracy posts were not profitable. (5) Mean likes (1459.2 vs 941.8), followers (24,075.7 vs 68,192.2) and following (1322.8 vs 910.7) are engagement intensities compared by accuracy, not shares of misinformation exposure, so no per_capita_intensity row. Note the reported SDs of 1 with 95% CIs spanning ~0.4 units are implausible for these means - a reporting error worth flagging. (6) The paper states GPT-4.1 was used to summarize text during writing (Acknowledgments); coding itself is described as human.

rob.design: Cross-sectional formative content analysis. Two research members searched public Instagram for "hepatitis b" and "hep b" from December 2021 to January 2022 at varying times of day and days of week; top 55 posts per term collected (rank-truncated, algorithm-ordered), duplicates removed, final N=103 unique posts, post = unit of analysis, no missing data. 58 variables coded per post from screenshots plus the poster's profile, using an adapted OnC-M misinformation codebook from the team's prior Facebook/Instagram/Pinterest/Twitter studies. Two coding cycles: 10% double-coded inductively by two authors with consensus and a tiebreaker, then the codebook applied to the rest; accuracy judged by hepatology clinicians against current standards of care. No inter-rater reliability coefficient reported. Descriptive statistics with chi-square, Fisher exact and z tests, alpha .05, Stata 18. STROBE-reported; IRB-exempt (public data). Authors' stated limitations: small sample, cross-sectional snapshot, no link to health outcomes, engagement limited to likes (comments/shares unavailable).
